questions.q: Per this lesson, why is clever code that does something in the fewest possible characters usually a worse trade than slightly longer, clearer code?
options: Because Apex specifically forbids short variable names
Because the few seconds saved writing clever code are repaid many times over by every future reader who has to decode it
Because longer code always runs faster
Because clean code requires using exactly the same number of characters every time
questions.explain: The lesson's framing is that code is read far more often than it's written, so a small one-time savings at write time is outweighed by the repeated cost every future reader pays trying to understand unclear code.

questions.q: What naming convention does this lesson say Apex uses for class names, as shown by InvalidDiscountException from Lesson 11?
options: camelCase, where only the first word is lowercase
snake_case, with underscores between words
PascalCase, where every word is capitalized
ALL_CAPS with underscores
questions.explain: The lesson states Apex convention uses PascalCase for class names (Customer, InvalidDiscountException) and camelCase for variables and methods (orderCount, calculateDiscount).

questions.q: What is the practical test this lesson gives for identifying a DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) violation?
options: Whether the code uses more than ten lines
Whether changing a piece of logic would require finding and updating it in more than one place in the codebase
Whether the code contains any comments at all
Whether a method has more than one parameter
questions.explain: The lesson's practical test is specifically: if changing a piece of logic honestly requires updating more than one place, that logic belongs in a shared method instead, per the fix Lesson 7 introduced.

questions.q: According to this lesson, does DRY mean all repetition should be eliminated no matter what?
options: Yes, any two pieces of code that look even slightly similar must always be merged into one method
No -- DRY is specifically about not duplicating the same underlying logic; two pieces of code that merely look similar but represent genuinely different concepts don't need to be forced together
Yes, but only for methods with a void return type
DRY applies only to variable names, never to logic
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that DRY isn't about avoiding all repetition at any cost -- it targets duplicated underlying logic, not surface-level similarity between genuinely different concepts.

questions.q: Per this lesson, when does a comment 'earn its place' in code?
options: Only when it restates exactly what the next line of code does
When it explains why -- a non-obvious business rule or a deliberate workaround -- rather than what, which the code should already show on its own
Only when the code is written in all one line
Comments should never be used under any circumstances
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes a comment that merely restates the obvious (adds nothing) from one that explains a non-obvious why, such as a business rule -- and notes that a comment needed only because the code itself is unclear is often a sign the code should be rewritten instead.
